question.explanation:
Using a cofactor expansion along the $4$th column, we have

\begin{align*} \left| \begin{array}{cccc} 2 & -1 & 4 & {\color{red}0} \\ 3 & 1 & 2 & {\color{red}2} \\ -1 & 2 & 3 & {\color{red}0} \\ -3 & -2 & 5 & {\color{red}-1} \end{array} \right| &= {\color{red}0} \cdot {\color{black}C_{14}} +{\color{red}2} \cdot {\color{blue}C_{24}} +{\color{red}0} \cdot {\color{black}C_{34}} +{\color{red}(-1)} \cdot {\color{blue}C_{44}} \\[5pt] &= {\color{red}2} \cdot {\color{blue}(-1)^{2+4}\cdot \left| \begin{array}{ccc} 2 & -1 & 4 \\ -1 & 2 & 3 \\ -3 & -2 & 5 \end{array} \right| } + {\color{red}(-1)} \cdot {\color{blue}(-1)^{4+4}\cdot \left| \begin{array}{ccc} 2 & -1 & 4 \\ 3 & 1 & 2 \\ -1 & 2 & 3 \end{array} \right| } \\[5pt] &= 2 \cdot \left| \begin{array}{ccc} 2 & -1 & 4 \\ -1 & 2 & 3 \\ -3 & -2 & 5 \end{array} \right| - \left| \begin{array}{ccc} 2 & -1 & 4 \\ 3 & 1 & 2 \\ -1 & 2 & 3 \end{array} \right|. \end{align*}

example.title: Calculating a Determinant Using a Laplace Expansion Across a Column

question.explanation:
The $4$th row of the given matrix contains two zeros, more than any other row. So, using a Laplace expansion along the $4$th row, we have

\begin{align*} \begin{vmatrix} 2 & 1 & -2 & 3 \\ -1 & -1 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 1 \\ {\color{red}2} & {\color{red}0} & {\color{red}0} & {\color{red}3} \end{vmatrix} &= {\color{red}2} \cdot {\color{blue}C_{41}} +{\color{red}0} \cdot {\color{black}C_{42}} +{\color{red}0} \cdot {\color{black}C_{43}} +{\color{red}3} \cdot {\color{blue}C_{44}} \\ &= {\color{red}2} \cdot {\color{blue}(-1)^{4+1} \cdot \begin{vmatrix} 1 & -2 & 3 \\ -1 & 2 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 1 \end{vmatrix}} + {\color{red}3} \cdot {\color{blue}(-1)^{4+4}\cdot \begin{vmatrix} 2 & 1 & -2\\ -1 & -1 & 2\\ 0 & 1 & 1 \end{vmatrix}} \\[5pt] &= -2 \begin{vmatrix} 1 & -2 & 3 \\ -1 & 2 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 1 \end{vmatrix} + 3\begin{vmatrix} 2 & 1 & -2\\ -1 & -1 & 2\\ 0 & 1 & 1 \end{vmatrix}. \end{align*}

Now, computing the first $3 \times 3$ determinant by applying a Laplace expansion along the $2$nd row, we obtain:

\begin{align*} \begin{vmatrix} 1 & -2 & 3 \\ {\color{red}-1} & {\color{red}2} & {\color{red}0}\\ 1 & 1 & 1 \end{vmatrix} &= {\color{red}(-1)} \cdot {\color{blue}C_{21}} +{\color{red}2} \cdot {\color{blue}C_{22}} +{\color{red}0} \cdot {\color{blue}C_{23}} \\ &= {\color{red}(-1)} \cdot {\color{blue}(-1)^{2+1}\cdot \begin{vmatrix} -2 & 3 \\ 1 & 1 \end{vmatrix}} + {\color{red}2} \cdot {\color{blue}(-1)^{2+2} \cdot \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 3\\ 1 & 1 \end{vmatrix}} \\[5pt] &= \begin{vmatrix} -2 & 3 \\ 1 & 1 \end{vmatrix} + 2\begin{vmatrix} 1 & 3\\ 1 & 1 \end{vmatrix} \\[5pt] &= (-2-3) +2 (1-3) \\[5pt] &= -5 +2\cdot (-2) \\[5pt] &= -9 \end{align*}

Finally, we compute the second $3 \times 3$ determinant by applying a Laplace expansion along its $3$rd row:

\begin{align*} \begin{vmatrix} 2 & 1 & -2\\ -1 & -1 & 2\\ {\color{red}0} & {\color{red}1} & {\color{red}1} \end{vmatrix} &= {\color{red}0} \cdot {\color{black}C_{31}} +{\color{red}1} \cdot {\color{blue}C_{32}} +{\color{red}1} \cdot {\color{blue}C_{33}} \\ &= {\color{red}1} \cdot {\color{blue}(-1)^{3+2}\cdot \begin{vmatrix} 2 & -2 \\ -1 & 2 \end{vmatrix}} + {\color{red}1} \cdot {\color{blue}(-1)^{3+3} \cdot \begin{vmatrix} 2 & 1\\ -1 & -1 \end{vmatrix}} \\[5pt] &= -\begin{vmatrix} 2 & -2 \\ -1 & 2 \end{vmatrix} + \begin{vmatrix} 2 & 1\\ -1 & -1 \end{vmatrix} \\[5pt] &= -(4-2) + (-2+1) \\[5pt] &= -2+ (-1) \\[5pt] &= -3 \end{align*}

Therefore,

\[ \begin{vmatrix} 2 & 1 & -2 & 3 \\ -1 & -1 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 2& 0 & 0 & 3 \end{vmatrix} = -2\cdot (-9) + 3\cdot (-3) =18-9= 9. \]

example.title: Calculating a Determinant Using a Laplace Expansion Across a Row

question.explanation:
The $3$rd row of the matrix contains two zeros, more than any other row. So using a Laplace expansion along the $3$rd row, we have

\begin{align*} \left| \begin{array}{cccc} 2 & -1 & 1 & 3 \\ -2 & 5 & 1 & 2 \\ {\color{red}0} & {\color{red}4} & {\color{red}7} & {\color{red}0} \\ 5 & -2 & 4 & 3 \end{array} \right| &= {\color{red}0} \cdot {\color{black}C_{31}} +{\color{red}4} \cdot {\color{blue}C_{32}} +{\color{red}7} \cdot {\color{blue}C_{33}} +{\color{red}0} \cdot {\color{black}C_{34}} \\ &= {\color{red}4} \cdot {\color{blue}(-1)^{3+2} \cdot \left| \begin{array}{ccc} 2 & 1 & 3 \\ -2 & 1 & 2 \\ 5 & 4 & 3 \end{array} \right|} + {\color{red}7} \cdot {\color{blue}(-1)^{3+3} \cdot \left| \begin{array}{ccc} 2 & -1 & 3 \\ -2& 5 & 2 \\ 5 & -2 & 3 \end{array} \right|} \\[5pt] &= -4 \cdot \left| \begin{array}{ccc} 2 & 1 & 3 \\ -2 & 1 & 2 \\ 5 & 4 & 3 \end{array} \right| +7 \cdot \left| \begin{array}{ccc} 2 & -1 & 3 \\ -2& 5 & 2 \\ 5 & -2 & 3 \end{array} \right|. \end{align*}

example.title: Applying a Laplace Expansion Across a Row

question.text: Compute the following determinant using a cofactor expansion along the $2$nd row: \[ \left| \begin{array}{cccc} 0 & -2 & 0 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 7 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 5 & 0 \\ -2 & 4 & 0 & 0 \end{array} \right|. \]
question.explanation:
Using cofactor expansion along the $2$nd row, we have

\begin{align*} \left| \begin{array}{cccc} 0 & -2 & 0 & 3 \\ {\color{red}0} & {\color{red}0} & {\color{red}7} & {\color{red}0} \\ 1 & 0 & 5 & 0 \\ -2 & 4 & 0 & 0 \end{array} \right| &= {\color{red}0} \cdot {\color{black}C_{21}} + {\color{red}0} \cdot {\color{black}C_{22}} + {\color{red}7} \cdot {\color{blue}C_{23}} + {\color{red}0} \cdot {\color{black}C_{24}} \\ &= {\color{red}7} \cdot {\color{blue}(-1)^{2+3} \cdot \left| \begin{array}{ccc} 0 & -2 & 3 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ -2 & 4 & 0 \end{array} \right|} \\[5pt] &= -7\left| \begin{array}{ccc} 0 & -2 & 3 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ -2 & 4 & 0 \end{array} \right|. \end{align*}

Now, computing the $3 \times 3$ determinant by applying a Laplace expansion along the $2$nd row, we obtain:

\begin{align*} \left| \begin{array}{ccc} 0 & -2 & 3 \\ {\color{red}1} & {\color{red}0} & {\color{red}0} \\ -2 & 4 & 0 \end{array} \right| &= {\color{red}1} \cdot {\color{blue}C_{21}} + {\color{red}0} \cdot {\color{black}C_{22}} + {\color{red}0} \cdot {\color{black}C_{23}}\\ &= {\color{red}1} \cdot {\color{blue}(-1)^{2+1} \cdot \left| \begin{array}{cc} -2 & 3 \\ 4 & 0 \end{array} \right|} \\[5pt] &= (-1) \left| \begin{array}{cc} -2 & 3 \\ 4 & 0 \end{array} \right| \\[5pt] &= (-1) (-12) \\[5pt] &= 12 \end{align*}

Therefore,

\[ \left| \begin{array}{cccc} 0 & -2 & 0 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 7 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 5 & 0 \\ -2 & 4 & 0 & 0 \end{array} \right| = -7\cdot 12= -84. \]

question.explanation:
Using a cofactor expansion along the $3$rd column, we have

\begin{align*} \left| \begin{array}{cccc} 3 & 2& {\color{red}-2} & -2 \\ 1 & -1& {\color{red}0} & 3 \\ 2& 5 & {\color{red}0} & 1 \\ -2& 4 & {\color{red}1} & -2 \end{array} \right| &= {\color{red}(-2)} \cdot {\color{blue}C_{13}} +{\color{red}0} \cdot {\color{black}C_{23}} +{\color{red}0} \cdot {\color{black}C_{33}} +{\color{red}1} \cdot {\color{blue}C_{43}} \\[5pt] &= {\color{red}(-2)} \cdot {\color{blue}(-1)^{1+3} \left| \begin{array}{ccc} 1 & -1& 3 \\ 2& 5 &1 \\ -2& 4 & -2 \end{array} \right|} + {\color{red}1} \cdot {\color{blue}(-1)^{4+3}\cdot \left| \begin{array}{ccc} 3 & 2& -2 \\ 1 & -1& 3 \\ 2& 5 & 1 \end{array} \right|} \\[5pt] &= -2 \cdot \left| \begin{array}{ccc} 1 & -1& 3 \\ 2& 5 &1 \\ -2& 4 & -2 \end{array} \right| - \left| \begin{array}{ccc} 3 & 2& -2 \\ 1 & -1& 3 \\ 2& 5 & 1 \end{array} \right|. \end{align*}
